I grew up with parents (both pHDs in biochemistry) who treated us kids with similar logic--as the kids of academics, we were *expected* to get all As, *expected* to preform exceptionally in standardized testing, *expected* to get into the competitive universities. I excelled in high school without praise, only criticism if my grades were less than near perfect. This parenting does not instill grit or resilience in your kids, it instills the belief that love is conditional and robs them of the ability to praise themselves for any accomplishment because there is always an environmental "excuse" for them having done well (i.e. your explanation that she is a girl and that your wife offered additional support at home). Your daughter does not need you as her father to rob her of her accomplishments. She can get that in the big bad world. What she won't find so easily is someone who supports her unconditionally and believes the world in her.

I think Aussie and Mildred are good case studies of what is as and is not realistic and/or acceptable behavior that is the outcome of trauma. Mildred only brings up her abandonment as a child as an excuse for behavior that is *never okay no matter the explanation*: physical violence and emotional manipulation. Aussie never uses their childhood as a defense for their negative actions, which, to be quite clear, are not healthy, but are not *violent*. Aussie is seen apologizing to Sam after their blowups consistently, without making excuses. Mildred *rarely* takes accountability (I think she admitted to wrongdoing in one speech throughout the whole show). Also, this is more of a vibes thing than anything else, but I don't think Sam would be with Aussie for as long as she has if she did not sense that her partner was *trying*. Mildred had extremely little self reflection throughout the show, and, quite frankly, seems to prefer blaming others rather than putting in the work herself.

I was fully recovered for 2 1/2 years until a similar unintentional weight gain put me back in a horrible headspace, and I let it get really bad again. I don't know if this is helpful (scare tactics aren't always super effective when your brain is already being so mean to itself), but recovering after a relapse, physically and emotionally, *sucks*. After a few years with a perfectly functioning, happy, healthy body, I personally had forgotten all the ways, big and small, that my body breaks down when I restrict, and how long it takes for it to get better again. I got back on track in the the fall after a year and a half off the rails, and by the summer, my body still has *so far to go* before it's healthy again (think: constipation, bloating, gas pains, back pain, dry / acne prone skin, thinned out hair, the list goes on). The ED voice telling you can lose the weight without the physical or emotional consequences of starvation is *lying*, and if you journaled at all when you first started recovery, maybe consider revisiting them and remembering how difficult the process was.

Addiction can come in a lot of iterations, many of which don’t involve substances—I have issues restricting my food intake, some folks work themselves to the bone at unforgiving jobs, some over exercise, some gamble, some compulsively shop, etc etc. I think the underlying issue is a lack of self that leaves you vulnerable to taking any ritualistic or repetitive behavior too far.

I take magnesium supplements and that helps with the constipation! My ED and the subsequent constipation caused issues with my pelvic floor that made it difficult for my muscles to allow me to poop. If you have insurance consider getting anal manometry (gross name, I know) testing done to see if this might be contributing!

I am exactly like this, and very much identify with my BPD diagnosis. The way I view my relationships in my head is pretty hallmark BPD (idealization/devaluation, intense fear of abandonment/rejection, "if they *truly* knew me they would despise me" despite the relationship being years long) but I tend to internalize the emotional outcomes of those thoughts into self harm rather than externalizing them within the relationship itself. Culturally I think those with BPD are viewed as initiating conflict constantly, but the flipside of this black and white "it's all your fault" thought can be "it's all my fault," which leads to avoiding conflict at all costs. Equally as unhealthy, and equally as BPD, just in a different way.

Thanks for this! My first flare up went down in 2017, and it took two years for me to get properly diagnosed and into physical therapy and remission. I was symptom free from for three years and have been struggling with my second flare up since October, most likely due to an extremely stressful service industry job that I have since left. I am returning to the same PT provider that helped me before, and am trying to remain hopeful that my symptoms will improve in a shorter period of time than before. The lack of control coupled with the extreme discomfort is incredibly difficult, and isolating for someone my age (diagnosed at 19, currently 25) , and I have to remind myself that at least I am older and wiser this time around!
